stem: in the Gospel of John (chapter 3), which man comes to Jesus by night and is told he must be "born again," or "born from above"?
options: Nicodemus
Zacchaeus
Bartimaeus
Nathanael
why: John 3:1–8: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus by night. Jesus tells him that unless a person is born anothen (again, or from above) he cannot see the kingdom of God.

es.stem: en el Evangelio de Juan (capítulo 3), ¿qué hombre va a ver a Jesús de noche y oye que debe "nacer de nuevo", o "nacer de lo alto"?
options: Nicodemo
Zaqueo
Bartimeo
Natanael
es.why: Juan 3:1–8: Nicodemo, fariseo y principal entre los judíos, va a ver a Jesús de noche. Jesús le dice que quien no nace anothen (de nuevo, o de lo alto) no puede ver el reino de Dios.

stem: the word Eucharist, which many churches use for the Lord's Supper, comes from a Greek word. what does that Greek word mean?
options: breaking bread
sharing a meal
remembrance
giving thanks
why: Eucharistia is Greek for thanksgiving. At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and "gave thanks" (eucharistesas) before breaking it (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24).

es.stem: la palabra Eucaristía, que muchas iglesias usan para la Cena del Señor, viene de una palabra griega. ¿qué significa esa palabra griega?
options: partir el pan
compartir la mesa
el recuerdo
dar gracias
es.why: Eucharistia en griego significa acción de gracias. En la Última Cena, Jesús tomó el pan y "dio gracias" (eucharistesas) antes de partirlo (Lucas 22:19; 1 Corintios 11:24).

stem: in Luke's parable of the Good Samaritan, why would a Samaritan as the hero have surprised Jesus' first listeners?
options: Samaritans were Roman soldiers posted along that road
Samaritans and Judeans were related but long at odds
Samaritans were Temple priests from Jerusalem itself
Samaritans were known as robbers on the Jericho road
why: Luke 10:30–37: Samaritans shared the books of Moses with Judeans but worshipped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem, and the two peoples had centuries of hostility (compare John 4:9). The one who stops is from across that line.

es.stem: en la parábola del buen samaritano, en Lucas, ¿por qué un samaritano como héroe habría sorprendido a quienes oyeron primero a Jesús?
options: los samaritanos eran soldados romanos de ese camino
samaritanos y judíos eran parientes, pero enemistados
los samaritanos eran sacerdotes del Templo de Jerusalén
los samaritanos eran famosos asaltantes de ese camino
es.why: Lucas 10:30–37: los samaritanos compartían con los judíos los libros de Moisés, pero adoraban en el monte Guerizín y no en Jerusalén, y entre ambos pueblos había siglos de hostilidad (ver Juan 4:9). El que se detiene viene del otro lado de esa línea.

stem: in 2 Corinthians 12, Paul begs the Lord three times to take away his "thorn in the flesh." what does the answer he receives, "My grace is sufficient for thee," tell him?
options: the thorn goes away once his faith grows strong enough
the thorn is a test to overcome by his own strength
the thorn stays, but God's gift is enough to bear it
the thorn will be healed later, once his work is done
why: 2 Corinthians 12:7–10: the thorn is not taken away. The Lord answers, "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness," and Paul ends, "when I am weak, then am I strong." Grace (charis, a free gift) is enough inside the trouble, not by his own strength.

es.stem: en 2 Corintios 12, Pablo le ruega al Señor tres veces que le quite su "aguijón en la carne". ¿qué le dice la respuesta que recibe, "Bástate mi gracia"?
options: el aguijón se irá cuando su fe sea bastante fuerte
el aguijón es una prueba que vencer con su propia fuerza
el aguijón se queda, pero el don de Dios basta para llevarlo
el aguijón sanará más tarde, cuando termine su obra
es.why: 2 Corintios 12:7–10: el aguijón no se le quita. El Señor responde: "Bástate mi gracia; porque mi poder se perfecciona en la debilidad", y Pablo concluye: "cuando soy débil, entonces soy fuerte". La gracia (charis, un regalo gratuito) basta en medio de la dificultad, no por su propia fuerza.

stem: Paul's words "love is patient, love is kind" (1 Corinthians 13) are often read at weddings. who was he writing to when he first wrote them?
options: a young couple he married in Corinth
the Roman officials who held him in prison
the elders of the Temple in Jerusalem
a church in Corinth split by rivalries
why: 1 Corinthians was Paul's letter to the church he founded in Corinth, which was divided into factions (1:10–12) and quarreling over spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14). Chapter 13 sits in the middle of that correction.

es.stem: las palabras de Pablo "el amor es paciente, es bondadoso" (1 Corintios 13) se leen mucho en las bodas. ¿a quién le escribía cuando las escribió por primera vez?
options: a una pareja joven que casó en Corinto
a los oficiales romanos que lo tenían preso
a los ancianos del Templo de Jerusalén
a una iglesia de Corinto dividida en bandos
es.why: 1 Corintios es la carta de Pablo a la iglesia que él fundó en Corinto, dividida en bandos (1:10–12) y peleada por los dones espirituales (capítulos 12–14). El capítulo 13 está en medio de esa corrección.

stem: a woman thinks it is unfair that her sister, who left the family and wasted her inheritance, is welcomed home with a party. in Luke's parable of the Prodigal Son, whose reaction is most like hers?
options: the younger son
the older brother
the hired servants
the father himself
why: Luke 15:25–32: the older son hears the music, is angry and will not go in, saying he never got even a young goat for a party. The father answers that his brother "was lost, and is found."

es.stem: una mujer piensa que es injusto que a su hermana, que dejó a la familia y malgastó su herencia, la reciban en casa con una fiesta. en la parábola del hijo pródigo, en Lucas, ¿la reacción de quién se parece más a la de ella?
options: el hijo menor
el hermano mayor
los jornaleros
el padre mismo
es.why: Lucas 15:25–32: el hijo mayor oye la música, se enoja y no quiere entrar, diciendo que nunca le dieron ni un cabrito para hacer fiesta. El padre responde que su hermano "se había perdido, y es hallado".

stem: some churches baptize babies, while others baptize only people old enough to profess faith for themselves. what reason does each side give?
why: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants: God's promise comes before the child can answer, whole households were baptized in Acts, and the family promises to raise the child in faith. Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize believers who can say yes themselves, often by immersion, matching Paul's picture of burial and rising (Romans 6:3–4).

rubric.point: gives a reason for infant baptism: God's grace or promise comes first, before the child can respond; or households were baptized in Acts; or the family and church promise to raise the child in faith. "tradition" alone does not count.

gives a reason for believer's baptism: it follows a person's own profession or choice of faith, so the person must be old enough to say yes. "babies are too young" counts only if it ties baptism to the person's own faith.
mentions immersion as burial and rising (Romans 6), names churches on either side, or notes that churches also differ on whether baptism itself saves or is an outward sign.

es.stem: algunas iglesias bautizan bebés, y otras solo bautizan a personas con edad para profesar la fe por sí mismas. ¿qué razón da cada lado?
es.why: Las iglesias católica, ortodoxa, luterana, anglicana, metodista y presbiteriana bautizan bebés: la promesa de Dios llega antes de que el niño pueda responder, en Hechos se bautizaban familias enteras, y la familia promete criar al niño en la fe. Las iglesias bautistas, pentecostales y muchas no denominacionales bautizan a creyentes que pueden decir que sí por sí mismos, a menudo por inmersión, como la imagen de Pablo de sepultura y resurrección (Romanos 6:3–4).

stem: in the Roman world, the cross was a means of execution. why was it a shocking symbol for the first Christians, and why did Christians come to treat it as the center of their faith?
why: Rome used crucifixion for slaves, rebels and threats to order: slow, public and shameful, so Paul calls the cross "a stumblingblock" and "foolishness" to many (1 Corinthians 1:23). Christians teach that on the cross Jesus gave his life for the world, and that his death was followed by the resurrection, so the sign of death became a sign of God's love and of life beyond it.

rubric.point: says crucifixion was a cruel, public and shameful Roman execution (for slaves, rebels or criminals), so honoring it seemed scandalous. saying only "it was sad" does not count.
gives the Christian reason it became central: Jesus' self-giving or sacrificial death for others (forgiveness, salvation, God's love), and/or that the resurrection showed death was not the end.

mentions Paul's "stumbling block / foolishness" (1 Corinthians 1:23), the charge "King of the Jews," Jesus' words from the cross, or that the earliest Christian art more often used other signs like the fish.

es.stem: en el mundo romano, la cruz era un medio de ejecución. ¿por qué era un símbolo escandaloso para los primeros cristianos, y por qué los cristianos llegaron a verla como el centro de su fe?
es.why: Roma usaba la crucifixión para esclavos, rebeldes y amenazas al orden: lenta, pública y vergonzosa; por eso Pablo dice que la cruz es "tropezadero" y "locura" para muchos (1 Corintios 1:23). Los cristianos enseñan que en la cruz Jesús dio su vida por el mundo, y que a su muerte siguió la resurrección; así, la señal de muerte se volvió señal del amor de Dios y de la vida más allá de ella.
